evidence_quotes.quote: For the sake of clarity, by basic sanitation services, we mean ‘the prescribed minimum standard of services necessary for the safe, hygienic and adequate collection, removal, disposal or purification of human excreta, domestic waste-water and sewage from households, including informal households’
For this reason, the discussion seeks to explore how courts are holding local government legally accountable for failures in delivering sanitation services.

Even where private property is concerned, the duty of local government is not suspended. The boundaries of private property cannot be used by local governments as a bar to fulfil their duties, yet private property owners cannot unreasonably restrict local governments from fulfilling their duties.

In Section 3, we explore how the legal obligations have found expression in judicial settings through a synopsis of some of the cases in which legal accountability has been pursued and where courts have had the opportunity to adjudicate on local government failures in sanitation services delivery.

Against this combined background, it is now necessary to sketch how the courts have facilitated legal accountability for failure to deliver on sanitation services. Such endeavour is pursued through the lens of four cases: Nokotyana, Beja, Kenton and Msunduzi.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines municipal delivery of and resident access to basic household and community sanitation services (VIP latrines, enclosed toilets, sewage reticulation maintenance) across informal settlements, towns, and private farms in South Africa.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading in subject matter. Under the plain wording, it examines constitutional, statutory, and judicial accountability frameworks governing municipal sanitation provision. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it examines specific rule-type mechanisms directly governing sanitation access: judicial enforcement remedies (structural interdicts and Municipal Manager contempt liability), formal township-upgrading preconditions for sanitation provision (Nokotyana), and private-land tenure/landowner-consent rules alongside statutory municipal takeover duties for farm occupiers under the Water Services Act s 26(3) and the Extension of Security of Tenure Act (Mshengu).
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05). Published explicitly as a 'CASE NOTE', the article is a pure doctrinal legal analysis of South African constitutional/statutory provisions and four reported court judgments (Nokotyana, Beja, Kenton, and Mshengu/Msunduzi). It collects no primary quantitative or qualitative data, applies no socio-legal empirical methodology, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not measure or report an empirical service-access outcome; instead, it doctrinally reviews judicial reasoning, legal accountability standards, and court-ordered remedies (such as structural interdicts) in four reported sanitation cases.
criterion_notes.c5: As a purely doctrinal case note reviewing statutory mandates and four appellate/High Court decisions, it lacks an empirical study population/sample, empirical exposure-outcome measurement, and empirical study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

population_and_sample: Four reported South African judicial decisions (Nokotyana, Beja, Kenton on Sea, and Mshengu/Msunduzi); no empirical population or sample
exposure: Constitutional and statutory municipal sanitation mandates, township-upgrading and private-land tenure rules, and judicial enforcement mechanisms (structural interdicts and contempt orders)
outcome: Doctrinal assessment of judicial accountability holdings and court-ordered remedies for municipal non-delivery of sanitation services (no empirical access outcome measured)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the article examines sanitation service access in South Africa (c1 = yes) and addresses rule-type legal enforcement, formal upgrading preconditions, and private-land tenure rules governing municipal sanitation duties (c2 = yes under both plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings), it is a pure doctrinal legal commentary ('CASE NOTE') analyzing constitutional/statutory provisions and four reported court judgments without any primary empirical data, empirical socio-legal methodology, or systematic empirical synthesis. Per Exclusion Criterion 1, pure doctrinal commentary without empirical access evidence is excluded.
